claims.text: In CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C, the identity of X controls metal-cation diffusion rates.
In CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C, the identity of X controls oxygen diffusion.
The X-dependent diffusion behavior governs whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms.
Si and Al form slowly growing, high-melting, stoichiometrically congruent oxides in the proposed alloy systems.
Slow oxide growth associated with Si or Al produces uniform scales with low internal stress.
The low-stress Si- or Al-associated oxide scales remain adherent during high-temperature exposure.
Mn promotes faster diffusion and less-controlled oxide-scale growth.
Fast, uncontrolled scale growth in Mn-containing alloys produces higher internal or thermal stresses.
The higher stresses in Mn-associated oxide scales cause cracking or spallation.
The oxidizing-surface microstructure is mediated by cation and oxygen diffusion modified by X.
Si- and Al-containing oxides have a favorable lattice-parameter match with the underlying metal.
Favorable oxide–metal lattice matching reduces interfacial stress and promotes scale adherence.
Under identical high-temperature exposures, Si-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys will form continuous, well-adherent, stable oxide layers.
Under identical high-temperature exposures, Al-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys will form continuous, well-adherent, stable oxide layers.
Under identical high-temperature exposures, Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys will form discontinuous, cracked, or spalled oxide scales.
CrFeCoNi without a reactive X forms a less robust oxide layer than corresponding Si- or Al-containing alloys.
The proposed mechanism applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Significant microstructural or environmental changes may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
